summary: 14-day closed-loop (AAPS) data show good overall glycemic control (86% TIR, 5.1% TBR, 8.9% TAR) with two distinct safety concerns: (1) pronounced afternoon hyperglycemic window (10:00–17:00 local; TAR 13–32%) and (2) evening low clusters (42–51 mg/dL, hour 17–19 local, Aug 13–14, 16, 21) caused by over-correction of the afternoon peak. Automation (SMB, UAM, high temps) is active and compensating, but data quality is excellent and profile is complete, allowing direct assessment. Zero meal logs, zero e-carbs, and no declared meal strategy mean meal bolusing is entirely reactive and driven by loop detection (UAM). The user is likely relying on closed-loop to handle meals rather than preplanning boluses. GLP-1 injections (Aug 14, 17, 20) are noted but appetite/meal-size effects are unquantified. Primary recommendation: increase basal in the 10:00–17:00 window and reduce max_iob to address the afternoon hyperglycemia and evening low cycle, while meal strategy is clarified through logging. Secondary: monitor DIA 10h and low-cluster pattern after changes.

analysis_steps.findings: ISF 56 mg/dL/U (single segment, all hours) is plausible but cannot be validated without isolated corrections. Therapy response windows show high variance in small-bolus responses (0.05–0.25 U), ranging from −53 to +135 mg/dL at 240 min; variance is likely from unlogged meal carbs, not ISF error. Larger boluses (≥0.45 U) produce expected drops (~80–100 mg/dL fall over 4 hours), consistent with ISF 56 and DIA 10h. CR segments (13 g/U overnight, 11.1 g/U early morning, 13.2 g/U daytime, 10.5 g/U afternoon, 12.6 g/U evening) are reasonable structure but daytime segment 13.2 g/U (08:00–16:00) may be too insensitive if afternoon meals are large (30–50 g carbs) and under-bolused (0.2 U observed). DIA 10 hours is long; carryover from evening boluses suppresses hour 01 basal (TBR 18.5%), but without DIA comparison testing, cannot confirm it is incorrect. DIA 10h is longer than oref0/oref1 defaults (4–6 h) but dilute insulin formulation (Aug 13 profile note) may justify longer DIA. Dynamic ISF is enabled (70% adjustment factor); sensitivity ratios mostly neutral (1.0), suggesting ISF is approximately correct on average or meals are masking the ISF error.

analysis_steps.findings: Autosens is disabled (autosens_enabled=false), preventing 24-hour adaptive learning of ISF/CR. Dynamic ISF is enabled (enabled=true, adjustment_factor_percent=70%), allowing real-time per-loop-cycle ISF modulation (±30% range). Observed sensitivity ratios are mostly neutral (1.0), with one instance 0.79 (more aggressive). Max_basal 12 U/h is very high (15–20× profile basal of 0.6–0.8 U/h); loop regularly uses 2–4 U/h temps during afternoon hyperglycemia, indicating high temps are necessary to correct inadequate profile basal or unbolused meals. Max_iob 25 U is moderate-to-high (approximately 1.3× daily insulin); IOB accumulation 4–6 U in afternoon/evening suggests max_iob is too high for a user on GLP-1 (appetite suppression may reduce expected meal carbs, leaving IOB to persist longer than designed). Autosens disabled is intentional (Aug 13 profile switch to 'u200 dilute basal'); protects new profile from over-adjustment but prevents detection of systematic profile errors (afternoon hyperglycemia pattern present Aug 8 onward, before and after switch). Dynamic ISF is working but not preventing afternoon hyperglycemia (TAR 13–32% persists), suggesting profile (basal/CR), not sensitivity adjustment, is the limiting factor. Safety limits are appropriate in absolute terms but contribute to low-cluster risk via IOB accumulation.

analysis_steps.findings: User has not declared a meal strategy (analysis_context.meal_strategies: empty, strategy_stable_for_period: null). Zero meal logs (carb_treatment_entries: 0) mean all meal handling is reactive and inferred from glucose response. Therapy response windows show 24 bolus events, most 0.05–0.25 U (small), with BG rising 50–135 mg/dL within 60–180 min after bolus despite insulin dosing. This pattern indicates meals are eaten during or after bolus, not before (no prebolus window evident). Meal boluses are small (~10–30% of CR-estimated need), suggesting either (1) meals are small (10–15 g carbs, consistent with GLP-1 appetite suppression), or (2) meals are larger but user is under-bolusing intentionally, relying on loop (SMB/UAM/temps) for coverage. Large bolus events (2.4 U, 0.65 U, 0.45 U) are rare (4 instances); 2.4 U on Aug 15 at BG 181 is followed by BG nadir 94 at 120m then rise to 130–188 by 240m (consistent with meal bolus + carb absorption). Aug 19, 0.65 U at BG 264 is followed by sustained drop to 96–103 mg/dL (consistent with correction bolus, no meal). Bolus response variance is high; small boluses show little visible effect (likely masked by concurrent meal carbs or sensor noise). GLP-1 notes (Aug 14, 17, 20) suggest appetite suppression, but meal size/timing changes are not documented.

analysis_steps.findings: Data quality is excellent; profile is complete and internally consistent. Two distinct, interconnected safety issues: (1) Afternoon hyperglycemia (10:00–17:00 local, TAR 13–32%, avg 148–162 mg/dL) persists despite SMB, UAM, and high temps (2–4 U/h), indicating profile basal is insufficient in the 10:00–16:00 window and/or meals are unbolused/under-bolused. (2) Evening low clusters (42–51 mg/dL, hour 17–19 local) occur 3–4 hours after afternoon peak, caused by aggressive loop overcorrection due to high IOB accumulation (4–6 U by late afternoon). Root causes and safe remediation pathway: (A) Afternoon hyperglycemia is likely caused by basal insufficiency (observed temps 2–4 U/h are 3–8× profile basal 0.5–0.8 U/h) combined with unknown meal bolus strategy (zero logs; UAM compensating). (B) Evening lows are caused by IOB accumulation (max_iob 25 U is too high for a user on GLP-1 with reduced meal intake; DIA 10h is long, carrying IOB across afternoon peak into evening). (C) Afternoon hyperglycemia -> high temps -> high IOB -> overcorrection -> lows. Safe order of changes: (1) Reduce max_iob 25→15–20 U (limits IOB, reduces overcorrection risk, improves low-cluster safety immediately). (2) Increase basal in 10:00–16:00 window from 0.7 U/h to 0.9–1.0 U/h (addresses afternoon hyperglycemia with reduced reliance on high temps; allows lower IOB to suffice). (3) Clarify meal strategy through 5–7 days of meal logging (resolves whether CR 13.2 g/U or immediate bolus % needs adjustment). (4) Monitor low-cluster pattern after max_iob reduction; if lows persist, reassess DIA 10h (long, may require shortening via separate test). Automation (SMB, UAM, Dynamic ISF) is working appropriately and should not be changed; it is compensating for profile defects, not creating them. Autosens remains disabled (protects recent profile switch); monitor for stabilization (typical 5–7 days post-switch; afternoon hyperglycemia predates switch by 6+ days, suggesting may not be pure 'new profile settling' effect). Overall strategy is reactive and loop-driven (small immediate boluses, SMB/UAM for coverage), consistent with GLP-1 appetite suppression and closed-loop automation. No e-carbs in use (appropriate for observed meal absorption 60–180m). Primary lever: profile basal and max_iob. Secondary lever: meal strategy clarification (logs). Tertiary lever: DIA reassessment (only if lows persist after max_iob reduction).
analysis_steps.evidence: Data quality: 98.7% coverage, zero defects. Safety events: hour 16 TAR 32.1%, hour 17 min 51 mg/dL; 16 readings ≤51 mg/dL, cluster timing 3–4h post-peak. Automation: SMB every 3 min, temps 2–4 U/h observed, IOB 4–6 U in afternoon/evening. Profile: basal 0.5–0.8 U/h (profile) vs. 2–4 U/h (observed temps). Meal strategy: zero logs, small boluses 0.1–0.2 U typical, large boluses 0.45–2.4 U rare. GLP-1: Aug 14, 17, 20 notes. Automation assessment: SMB/UAM/temps are compensating, not causing. Hypoglycemia pattern: Aug 13–14, 16, 21 low clusters at 18:00–19:00 local (5 hours after hour 14 peak). IOB evidence: Aug 19 4.73 U, Aug 21 5.935 U recorded.

Max_iob reduction is independent and safe (addresses evening low risk). Meal strategy change depends on logs. strengths: Excellent data quality (98.7% CGM coverage, zero defects, complete profile).
Clear identification of two linked safety issues (afternoon hyperglycemia → evening low cluster) with straightforward root causes (insufficient basal + high IOB accumulation).
Automation is functioning correctly (SMB, UAM, Dynamic ISF, high temps) and can be adjusted safely without disabling.
Profile structure is reasonable and complete; no internal contradictions.
Low overall TBR (5.1%) and good TIR (86%) demonstrate that the system is not fundamentally broken; targeted changes should improve control without destabilizing the rest.
GLP-1 use is documented (dates), providing context for suspected meal-size reduction.
Safe change pathway is sequential (max_iob first, then basal, then meal logs, then conditional DIA test), reducing risk of cascading errors.
issues: Zero meal logs: Cannot distinguish meal-driven afternoon hyperglycemia from basal insufficiency.
Zero e-carb entries: Unclear whether this is intentional (all meals simple carbs) or user has not enabled the feature.
No declared meal strategy: Meal bolusing is entirely reactive and loop-driven; unclear whether small immediate boluses (0.1–0.2 U typical) are intentional or under-conservative.
GLP-1 effect on appetite/meal size not quantified: Notes record doses (Aug 14, 17, 20) but not resulting meal-size changes.
Evening low clusters are safety events (42–51 mg/dL) caused by overcorrection; require intervention before other optimizations.
High IOB accumulation (4–6 U in afternoon/evening) is contributing to low-cluster risk and overshooting; max_iob 25 is too high for this user.
Afternoon hyperglycemia (TAR 13–32%, hour 10–17) persists despite automation; profile basal likely insufficient.
DIA 10 hours is long and unvalidated; IOB carryover into morning and evening creates risk of cascading overcorrections.
Autosens disabled prevents adaptive learning; unable to auto-detect whether ISF/CR are drifting (intentional to protect recent profile switch, but masks systematic errors).

recommendations.title: Reduce max IOB to limit afternoon IOB accumulation and evening overcorrection lows
recommendations.description: Max IOB 25 U is too high for this user (represents 1.3× daily insulin; IOB regularly 4–6 U in afternoon, contributing to evening low clusters 42–51 mg/dL at hour 17–19). Reducing max_iob to 15–20 U will limit IOB accumulation, reduce aggressive loop correction, and lower risk of overcorrection lows. This change is independent of meal strategy and basal and addresses evening safety immediately. Make this change first, before increasing basal.

suggested_change.rationale: Limits IOB to ~0.9× daily insulin (18/19.7), conservative for closed-loop safety. Conservative estimate accounts for GLP-1 effect (smaller meals) reducing expected insulin demand.

recommendations.title: Increase basal in 10:00–16:00 window to address persistent afternoon hyperglycemia
recommendations.description: Afternoon hyperglycemia (TAR 13–32%, avg 148–162 mg/dL, hour 10–17 local) persists despite SMB, UAM, and high temps (2–4 U/h, which are 3–8× profile basal). Observed loop temps indicate profile basal 0.7 U/h in this window is insufficient. Increase to 0.9–1.0 U/h will provide more basal coverage, reduce reliance on high temps, and lower IOB accumulation (enabling the reduced max_iob to be effective). This change is safe only after confirming it is not meal-driven (see meal logging, next). Monitor for overnight lows; if TBR increases after change, reassess.

suggested_change.rationale: Addresses observed temps 2–4 U/h by increasing baseline. Conservative increment (0.2 U/h ≈ 30% increase) reduces overcorrection risk. If afternoon hyperglycemia persists or worsens after 3–5 days, revert and investigate meal strategy.

recommendations.title: Log all meals for 5–7 days to clarify bolus strategy and resolve CR adequacy
recommendations.description: Zero meal logs prevent validation of CR (13.2 g/U daytime) and assessment of immediate bolus percentage. Observed meal boluses are small (0.1–0.2 U typical), but without carb amounts, cannot determine if meals are small (10–15 g, consistent with GLP-1 appetite suppression) or if boluses are under-conservative. Log carb amount, meal timing (start of meal), bolus timing (pre/during/after meal), and bolus amount. This will reveal whether CR needs adjustment and whether immediate bolus % should increase. Conditional on basal and max_iob changes; needed to finalize meal strategy.

suggested_change.proposed_value: 5–7 days of meal logs (carbs, timing, bolus size, timing)
suggested_change.rationale: Resolves whether afternoon hyperglycemia is basal insufficiency (confirmed via basal test) or CR insufficiency (found via meal logs). Enables decision on whether to increase immediate bolus %, use e-carbs, or accept loop-driven coverage.

recommendations.title: Re-enable Autosens after profile stabilization (5–7 days post-switch, around Aug 20–21) if afternoon hyperglycemia persists
recommendations.description: Autosens is disabled to protect the Aug 13 profile switch ('u200 dilute basal'). However, afternoon hyperglycemia pattern is visible Aug 8 onward (pre-switch) and Aug 10–14 (post-switch), suggesting it may not be entirely a 'new profile settling' effect. After 5–7 days (typical stabilization window), if TAR remains elevated despite basal increase and meal clarification, consider re-enabling Autosens to allow 24-h adaptive ISF/CR adjustment. Monitored re-enable (not automatic); assess response over 3–5 days before finalizing.

suggested_change.rationale: Enables adaptive learning of ISF/CR if profile changes do not resolve afternoon hyperglycemia. Conservative: re-enable only after data clarification (meal logs, basal response) to avoid conflating basal adjustment with Autosens adaptation.

recommendations.title: Monitor low-cluster pattern after max_iob reduction; if lows persist, consider DIA validation testing (not routine change)
recommendations.description: DIA 10 hours is long and unvalidated. It causes IOB carryover into morning (hour 01 TBR 18.5%) and contributes to evening low-cluster overcorrection (high IOB persists 3–4 hours post-afternoon-peak). After reducing max_iob and increasing basal, monitor whether evening low clusters improve. If low-cluster frequency remains high (>2 events per week) despite max_iob reduction, DIA 10 may be too long; shorter DIA (6–8 hours) may reduce IOB carryover. However, DIA change is complex (affects all corrections, not just afternoon) and dilute insulin may require longer DIA. Only pursue if low pattern does not improve after other changes. Requires controlled test: fasting state, single correction bolus, glucose observation 8+ hours.

suggested_change.proposed_value: test alternative 6–8 h only if low-cluster pattern persists post-max_iob reduction
suggested_change.rationale: Low-cluster pattern is likely caused primarily by IOB accumulation (addressed by max_iob reduction), not DIA. DIA change is secondary and should only be pursued if evening lows do not improve within 5–7 days of max_iob reduction.

profile_recommendation.recommendation: Reduce max_iob from 25 U to 18 U; increase basal in 10:00–16:00 window from 0.7 U/h to 0.9 U/h. Change max_iob first (safety), then basal (target hyperglycemia), separated by 1 day minimum. Monitor for overnight lows and evening low-cluster improvement. Continue daily glucose review for 5–7 days after each change. After basal change settles (3–5 days), log meals for 5–7 days to validate CR and immediate bolus percentage. education.topic: Why afternoon hyperglycemia persists despite closed-loop automation
education.explanation: The loop's SMB (small boluses every 3 min) and high temperature basals (2–4 U/h) are designed to correct glucose when it rises unexpectedly. However, they work reactively—they see the glucose rising and respond. If the basal insulin rate itself is too low for the fasting state, or if meals are not bolused in advance (prebolus), the loop is always 'chasing' the rise and cannot prevent it. In your case, afternoon average glucose (148–162 mg/dL in hours 14–17) is staying high because profile basal (0.7 U/h) is insufficient for that time of day. The loop compensates with high temps (2–4 U/h, 3–8× the profile rate), but this creates high insulin-on-board (IOB), which then causes the evening overcorrection lows. By increasing your profile basal to 0.9 U/h, you are providing more insulin 'up front,' so the loop does not need to use high temps to correct, IOB stays lower, and evening lows are reduced.

Insulin-on-board (IOB) is the amount of insulin still acting in your body from previous boluses. If IOB accumulates too high (your system allowed up to 25 U), and then glucose starts to fall in the evening, the loop sees the fall and reduces basal to prevent lows. However, with 25 U IOB, the loop may over-reduce (or even stop basal entirely), causing glucose to drop too far. By reducing max_iob to 18 U, you are capping the amount of insulin that can accumulate, so the evening correction is less aggressive and less likely to overshoot into lows. This is especially important for you because GLP-1 may reduce meal size, meaning IOB from afternoon boluses persists longer than the system expects.

Without meal logs, the system cannot tell whether your afternoon highs are caused by basal being too low, or meals being too large and under-bolused. Your profile carb ratio says 1 unit covers 13.2 grams of carbs, but if you are not logging carbs, the loop cannot use this information. Instead, it detects rising glucose (via UAM) and delivers insulin reactively. By logging meals for 5–7 days, you will show exactly how much carb you eat at each meal and how much insulin you bolus. This reveals whether your carb ratio is correct (e.g., a 30-gram meal should receive ~2.3 units; if you are giving 0.2 units, either the meal is small or the bolus is too small). This data also helps you and your care team decide whether to adjust bolus percentage, carb ratio, or continue relying on the loop to handle meals.

education.topic: Prebolus and immediate bolus percentage explained
education.explanation: A prebolus is when you give insulin 10–15 minutes before eating, allowing it to start working before carbs enter your bloodstream. This prevents the 'glucose spike' that occurs when carbs are absorbed faster than insulin can cover. An immediate bolus percentage is the fraction of your total meal bolus (calculated from carb amount and carb ratio) that you give upfront; the rest can come from SMB during meal absorption. For example, if a meal needs 2 units total, a 50% immediate bolus means you give 1 unit now and let the loop add 0.5–1 unit via SMB as glucose rises. Your current strategy gives very small boluses (0.1–0.2 U), suggesting either meals are very small or you are relying entirely on the loop (SMB/UAM) to handle them. Both are valid with closed-loop, but clarity helps you and your team optimize.

education.topic: Dynamic ISF and why it does not prevent high BG
education.explanation: Dynamic ISF adjusts your insulin sensitivity every loop cycle (every 5 minutes) based on how your glucose is changing. If glucose is rising faster than expected, Dynamic ISF can make insulin more sensitive (stronger effect per unit), pushing the loop to give more insulin. However, Dynamic ISF works within the constraints of your profile and automation settings. If your basal is too low or meals are unbolused, no amount of Dynamic ISF adjustment can prevent the rise—it can only slow it or shorten the time to peak. Think of it as 'tweaking' sensitivity in real-time, not fixing a fundamental profile problem. This is why basal and meal strategy are primary levers; automation adjustments are secondary.

GLP-1 medications (like semaglutide) slow stomach emptying and reduce appetite, which typically means smaller meal sizes and delayed carb absorption. Your system was configured before starting GLP-1, so profile settings (basal, carb ratio) may not account for the new meal patterns. As your appetite adjusts and meal sizes change, the loop adapts (via SMB/UAM), but profile settings may need tweaking. This is why Autosens (24-hour learning) can be helpful after your profile stabilizes—it detects that your meals are smaller and adjusts carb ratio accordingly. For now, meal logging will show exactly how GLP-1 is affecting your eating, allowing manual adjustment if needed.

safety_notes.content: This analysis is for decision support and educational purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice. You must independently verify every proposed change with your healthcare team, make changes one at a time, and monitor glucose closely. Do not change settings automatically; review each recommendation and discuss with your care team before implementing.

Change one parameter at a time, separated by at least 24 hours (or as directed by your care team). This allows you to observe the effect of each change clearly. If you change multiple parameters simultaneously (e.g., basal and max_iob on the same day), you cannot tell which change caused any improvement or worsening. Recommended order: (1) max_iob reduction first (immediate safety benefit), (2) basal increase next day, (3) meal logging concurrent, (4) CR adjustment conditional on meal log findings.

If you increase basal in the 10:00–16:00 window from 0.7 to 0.9 U/h, monitor your overnight and early-morning glucose (hours 00–08 local, approximately 23:00–07:00 UTC). If your time below 70 mg/dL increases significantly (>10% of the time) or you experience frequent low alarms overnight, your basal increase may be too aggressive. In that case, revert to 0.7 U/h or try a smaller increment (0.8 U/h). Report changes in overnight lows to your care team immediately.

safety_notes.category: Verify evening low reduction after max_iob change
safety_notes.content: After reducing max_iob from 25 to 18 U, you should observe fewer severe low events (readings <51 mg/dL) in the afternoon and evening (hours 16–20 local). If the frequency of severe lows does not decrease within 5–7 days, this change alone may not be sufficient; the problem may be in basal insufficiency, meal bolusing, or DIA. Continue with the basal increase as planned and proceed to meal logging. If severe lows persist after both changes, escalate to your care team for DIA assessment or alternative interventions.

safety_notes.category: Meal logging is essential for validation
safety_notes.content: The afternoon hyperglycemia (TAR 13–32%, hours 10–17) could be caused by insufficient basal, insufficient meal boluses, or both. Without meal logs, recommendations for basal are educated guesses. After you log meals for 5–7 days, you and your care team will have concrete data to decide whether basal increase alone is sufficient, or whether carb ratio or bolus strategy also need adjustment. DIA (duration of insulin action) is set to 10 hours in your profile. This is longer than typical (oref0/oref1 defaults are 4–6 hours) but may be correct for your dilute insulin formulation. Do not attempt to shorten DIA on your own without discussing with your care team. DIA affects every bolus and can have unintended consequences if not done carefully. If evening lows persist after max_iob reduction and basal increase, your care team can conduct a formal DIA test (giving a bolus in fasting state and observing glucose for 8+ hours).

Autosens is currently disabled (to protect the August 13 profile switch). If you decide to re-enable it (after profile stabilization, ~Aug 20–21 or later), do so only after consulting your care team. After re-enable, allow 3–5 days for Autosens to calculate and adjust ISF/CR; then evaluate whether afternoon hyperglycemia improves. If Autosens adjustments seem too aggressive (e.g., ISF drops too low, causing lows), you can disable it again.

Your system has recorded 16 readings ≤51 mg/dL over 14 days, with clusters at 42–51 mg/dL. This is a safety concern and is the primary reason for the max_iob reduction recommendation. Reducing max_iob should lower the frequency of these severe lows. If you continue to experience lows <60 mg/dL more than once per week despite these changes, contact your care team immediately. Frequent severe lows indicate a mismatch between insulin and carbohydrate intake that requires professional review.

GLP-1 reduces appetite and may slow carb absorption. As your body adjusts to GLP-1 (days to weeks), your meal patterns may shift. Monitor your glucose control closely during this adjustment period. If you experience a sustained improvement in afternoon control (TAR decreases further) without any setting changes, this may be the GLP-1 effect settling in; no action needed. If control worsens, report to your care team—GLP-1 dose or timing may need adjustment, or insulin settings may need re-evaluation.

This analysis assumes your pump and CGM are functioning reliably and are properly calibrated. If you experience frequent sensor errors, pump connection failures, or inconsistent readings, contact your device manufacturers and care team before making insulin adjustments. Reliable telemetry is essential for safe closed-loop operation and accurate profile tuning.
